welcome.txt.c:
Hi explorer,

I'm Tux, the Linux penguin. I need your help!

The Segfault Daemon stole my Kernel Crown and hid it somewhere
deep inside this computer. Only someone who knows the terminal
can get it back.

Start by going into the dungeon:   cd dungeon
Then look around with:             ls

Good luck!
  - Tux 🐧

linux-facts.txt.c:
Linux runs on all of the top 500 supercomputers.
Android is built on the Linux kernel.
The mascot Tux was drawn by Larry Ewing in 1996.
Linux is free: free as in price, and free as in freedom.

todo.txt.c:
- learn the terminal
- rescue the crown
- tell friends about Linux

about-tuxplore.txt.c:
TUXPLORE
========

You are playing Tuxplore: a game that teaches Linux by letting you use it.
TuxOS, the system you are in now, is pretend, but the commands are real.

What it is, what you will learn, and the FAQ:
  https://tuxplore.akashanil.dev/about.html

Public usage stats:
  https://tuxplore.akashanil.dev/stats.html

Made by Akash A.  Liked it? Tell a friend who is curious about Linux.

personal.txt.c: A personal file that migration must preserve.

README.txt.c:
Welcome to the Dungeon.

Adventurers who only look at the obvious miss the most important things.
In Linux, hidden files start with a dot.

Try:  ls -a

.map.c:
THE MAP
=======

The gate to the crypt needs a secret word.
The word is written in one of the books in library/.

There are too many books to read one by one.
Search them all at once:   grep -r secret library

Then open the gate:        ./gate.sh <the-secret-word>

the-first-penguin.txt.c:
Long ago, in 1991, a student named Linus wrote a small kernel.
He said it was "just a hobby, won't be big and professional".
Today it runs phones, servers, cars and even the International Space Station.

on-sharing.txt.c:
Richard Stallman began the GNU project in 1983.
He believed software should respect the people who use it.
GNU tools plus the Linux kernel made a complete, free operating system.

bestiary.txt.c:
GOBLIN: small, grumpy, lives in files. Weak against rm.
DAEMON: a background process. Most are friendly. One is not.
ZOMBIE: a process that finished but whose parent never noticed.

recipes.txt.c:
Penguin stew: do not make penguin stew.
Fish tacos: preferred by penguins everywhere.
Coffee: required by system administrators.

the-four-freedoms.txt.c:
Free software grants four freedoms:
0. Run the program for any purpose.
1. Study how it works and change it.
2. Share copies with others.
3. Share your improved versions.
The secret word for the gate is: freedom

distros.txt.c:
A distribution, or distro, is the Linux kernel bundled with tools and apps.
Debian, Fedora and Arch are families. Ubuntu and Mint grew from Debian.
There are hundreds of them, and that is a feature.

poetry.txt.c:
Roses are red,
terminals are black,
type rm -rf /
and there is no way back.

maps-and-paths.txt.c:
Paths that start with / are absolute: they start at the root.
Paths without / are relative: they start where you are.
.. means the parent directory. ~ means your home.

lost-and-found.txt.c:
Nothing to see here. The good stuff is elsewhere.
Try searching instead of reading every single book.

the-shell.txt.c:
The shell reads what you type and runs programs.
Bash is the most common one. Zsh and fish are popular too.
Press Tab to autocomplete. Press Up to repeat a command.

dragons.txt.c:
There are no dragons in this library.
There is, however, a very old printer that jams constantly.

permissions.txt.c:
Every file has permissions: read (r), write (w) and execute (x).
A script cannot run unless it has x. chmod +x adds it.
Type ls -l to see permissions.

diary.txt.c: Dear diary, someone took my crown. I am very sad. I ate a fish. I feel better.
